reason: The sources corroborate the discovery, extreme mechanics, and subsequent scientific debate over iron rain on WASP-76b across multiple independent reports.
story: In 2020, astronomers pointed the Very Large Telescope at WASP-76b, an ultra-hot gas giant 640 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. Tidally locked in a blistering 1.8-day orbit, one face of the planet permanently confronts its host star while the other sits in perpetual darkness. Dayside temperatures soar past 2,400 degrees Celsius, an inferno so severe that atmospheric molecules rip apart and metallic iron evaporates into gas. Ferocious winds sweep that iron vapor across the evening terminator into the cooler nightside, where temperatures plummet to around 1,500 degrees Celsius. Using the ESPRESSO spectrograph, scientists detected iron vapor entering the evening sector, but found nothing at dawn. Their conclusion was surreal: the vapor cools, condenses, and dumps torrential rains of molten liquid iron into the alien night. Though later models debate if cloud layers fully condense, WASP-76b proved planetary weather can be stranger than fiction.
angle: On the nightside of exoplanet WASP-76b, vaporized metal blown in from a dayside furnace cools down and falls as liquid iron rain.

claims.claim: WASP-76b is an ultra-hot gas giant exoplanet located in the constellation Pisces.
WASP-76b orbits its parent star once every 1.8 Earth days.
Intense stellar radiation puffs WASP-76b up to nearly twice the diameter of Jupiter.
WASP-76b is tidally locked to its host star, keeping one hemisphere in eternal daylight and the other in perpetual darkness.
Dayside temperatures on WASP-76b exceed 2,400 degrees Celsius (4,350 degrees Fahrenheit).
The dayside heat is intense enough to vaporize metals such as iron into the atmosphere.
Radiation on the dayside is so intense that molecules split apart into individual atoms.
WASP-76b receives thousands of times more radiation from its star than Earth receives from the Sun.
Temperatures on the nightside drop significantly to around 1,400 to 1,500 degrees Celsius.
The extreme temperature contrast between the day and night sides drives ferocious atmospheric winds carrying iron vapor to the nightside.
Astronomers using the ESPRESSO instrument on the Very Large Telescope in Chile detected a strong signature of iron vapor at the evening border.
No iron vapor signature was detected at the morning border where the nightside transitions to day.
Researchers concluded that iron vapor condenses in the cooler nightside atmosphere and falls as liquid iron rain.
The ESPRESSO science observations of WASP-76b were conducted in September 2018.
The study reporting the nightside iron condensation was led by David Ehrenreich of the University of Geneva.
Space telescope observations detected signatures of titanium oxide and water vapor in WASP-76b's atmosphere.
Follow-up high-resolution spectroscopy confirmed the presence of calcium in the atmosphere of WASP-76b.

disputed: Distance to WASP-76b: Earlier estimates stated 390 light-years, but updated Gaia measurements revised the distance to approximately 634 to 640 light-years; scripts should state around 640 light-years or mention the revision.

Occurrence of iron rain: While the 2020 ESPRESSO team interpreted the missing morning iron signal as liquid iron rain, subsequent 2020 and 2021 modeling noted the signal could arise from stellar light contamination and thermal variations without significant nightside iron precipitation; scripts should attribute the iron rain conclusion to the 2020 research team.
